facc-w1-q1.question: Ravi takes ₹5,000 from his cycle repair shop's cash box to buy groceries for his home. Which concept says this must be recorded as drawings, not as a business expense?
facc-w1-q1.explanation: The business entity concept treats the business and its owner as separate, so the owner's personal spending is drawings (equity falls), not an expense. Accrual only tells you when to record something, not whose spending it is.

facc-w1-q2.question: A business has total assets of ₹8,00,000 and total liabilities of ₹3,50,000. What is the owner's equity?
facc-w1-q2.explanation: Equity = Assets − Liabilities = 8,00,000 − 3,50,000 = ₹4,50,000. ₹11,50,000 comes from adding liabilities to assets — liabilities are outsiders' claims and must be subtracted.

facc-w1-q3.question: A consulting firm's financial year ends on 31 March. In March it delivered services worth ₹60,000, to be paid in April. Also in March it received a ₹10,000 advance for work to be done in April. Under the accrual concept, what is this year's (up to March) revenue?
facc-w1-q3.explanation: Revenue is recorded when earned: the ₹60,000 of services delivered in March is this year's revenue even though the cash comes later. The work for the ₹10,000 advance has not been done, so it is a liability. ₹70,000 comes from treating the advance as revenue too.

facc-w1-q4.question: At year-end a shop holds two items. Item X: cost ₹1,20,000, NRV ₹1,05,000. Item Y: cost ₹50,000, NRV ₹70,000. Apply the lower of cost and NRV rule item by item. What inventory figure appears in the balance sheet?
facc-w1-q4.explanation: Take the lower value for each item: X = min(1,20,000, 1,05,000) = 1,05,000; Y = min(50,000, 70,000) = 50,000. Total = ₹1,55,000. ₹1,70,000 comes from comparing total cost (1,70,000) with total NRV (1,75,000) — that hides X's ₹15,000 loss behind Y's gain.

facc-w1-q5.question: A factory machine would fetch only ₹40,000 as scrap today, but the balance sheet shows it at ₹3,00,000 (cost minus depreciation). Which assumption makes this correct?
facc-w1-q5.explanation: Going concern assumes the business will continue and keep using the machine, so it is shown at cost minus depreciation, not scrap value. Conservatism is the tempting trap, but it deals with uncertain losses — it does not mean writing a working machine down to scrap value.

facc-w1-q6.question: A business starts with Assets of ₹5,00,000 and Liabilities of ₹2,00,000. Then: (i) it pays creditors ₹40,000 in cash, (ii) it provides services worth ₹70,000 on credit, (iii) it pays rent of ₹15,000 in cash, (iv) the owner withdraws ₹10,000 for personal use. What is equity at the end?
facc-w1-q6.explanation: Opening equity = 5,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 3,00,000. Revenue +70,000, rent −15,000, drawings −10,000 ⇒ ₹3,45,000. Paying creditors cuts cash and liabilities by 40,000 each and leaves equity unchanged. ₹3,05,000 is the trap of also taking that 40,000 off equity; ₹3,55,000 comes from forgetting drawings. Check: assets 5,05,000 = liabilities 1,60,000 + equity 3,45,000.

facc-w2-q1.question: Which of these items is this month's **expense**, not an asset?
facc-w2-q1.explanation: This month's electricity has been used up this month and gives no future benefit, so it is an expense. Machinery and the patent will serve for several years (capital expenditure), and inventory will be sold later — all three are assets.

facc-w2-q2.question: Which statement about the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss is correct?
options: The balance sheet shows the position on a date; the P&L shows performance over a period
The balance sheet shows performance over a period; the P&L shows the position on a date
Both show the position on the same date, only the format differs
Assets and liabilities appear in the P&L, revenue in the balance sheet
facc-w2-q2.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot 'as at 31 March' — what is owned and owed on that day. The P&L covers 'the year ended 31 March' — what was earned and spent across the whole year. The second option is the reverse and is the most common confusion.

facc-w2-q3.question: A trading firm's items for the year: revenue ₹9,00,000; cost of goods sold ₹5,40,000; salaries ₹1,20,000; rent ₹60,000; purchase of a new delivery van ₹3,00,000; depreciation on the van ₹30,000; repayment of bank loan principal ₹50,000; loan interest ₹10,000. What is the profit for the year?
facc-w2-q3.explanation: Subtract only expenses: 9,00,000 − 5,40,000 − 1,20,000 − 60,000 − 30,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,40,000. The van purchase is capital expenditure (it becomes an asset; only depreciation goes to P&L) and principal repayment is not an expense. ₹90,000 comes from subtracting the repayment, −₹1,30,000 from expensing the van, ₹1,70,000 from forgetting depreciation.

facc-w2-q4.question: A company has total assets of ₹12,00,000. Current liabilities are ₹2,20,000, non-current liabilities ₹3,00,000 and share capital ₹5,00,000. What are reserves and surplus?
facc-w2-q4.explanation: Total equity = 12,00,000 − 2,20,000 − 3,00,000 = 6,80,000. Share capital is 5,00,000 of that, so reserves = ₹1,80,000. ₹6,80,000 is the whole of equity (share capital not removed), and ₹4,80,000 / ₹4,00,000 come from leaving out one type of liability.

facc-w2-q5.question: A bakery sells its old oven for ₹85,000. On the day of sale the oven's carrying amount (cost − depreciation) was ₹70,000. What appears in the statement of profit and loss?
options: Nothing, only the balance sheet changes
facc-w2-q5.explanation: Selling an oven is not the bakery's normal business, so the full ₹85,000 is not revenue. Only the gain = 85,000 − 70,000 = ₹15,000 (other income) goes to P&L. The sale price exceeds the carrying amount, so it is not a loss.

facc-w2-q6.question: A proprietor's opening equity was ₹4,00,000. During the year she introduced ₹1,00,000 of extra capital and made drawings of ₹30,000. Closing equity is ₹5,20,000. What was the profit for the year?
facc-w2-q6.explanation: Closing = Opening + capital introduced + profit − drawings ⇒ 5,20,000 = 4,00,000 + 1,00,000 + P − 30,000 ⇒ P = ₹50,000. ₹1,20,000 is just the change in equity (new capital is not profit); ₹20,000 comes from forgetting to add drawings back; ₹1,50,000 from forgetting to remove the new capital.

facc-w3-q1.question: Before 31 March a magazine publisher receives ₹1,20,000 of subscriptions for issues to be sent next year. In the 31 March balance sheet, what is this amount?
facc-w3-q1.explanation: The cash has come in but the obligation to deliver the magazines remains, so it is unearned revenue — a liability. Treating it as this year's revenue is the most common trap; revenue arises as the issues are sent.

facc-w3-q2.question: Staff worked in March; their ₹40,000 salary will be paid in April. The financial year ends on 31 March. What is the correct treatment?
options: A ₹40,000 expense in March, and a ₹40,000 liability on 31 March
An April expense, because the cash goes out in April
No entry until it is paid
facc-w3-q2.explanation: Accrual concept: the expense arises when the service is used — in March. It has not been paid yet, so an outstanding salary liability also arises. 'An April expense' is cash-basis thinking.

facc-w3-q3.question: On 1 January 2026 a shop paid ₹1,20,000 in advance as rent for a full 12 months. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What is prepaid rent in the 31 March 2026 balance sheet?
facc-w3-q3.explanation: Jan–Mar = 3 months belong to this year: expense = 1,20,000 × 3/12 = 30,000. The benefit of the other 9 months comes later: prepaid = 1,20,000 × 9/12 = ₹90,000. ₹30,000 is this year's expense, not the prepayment — the trap is swapping the two.

facc-w3-q4.question: On 1 August 2025 an online learning startup received ₹24,000 from a customer for a 12-month subscription. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. How much revenue is recognised in this financial year?
facc-w3-q4.explanation: Service was provided for 8 months, Aug to Mar: 24,000 × 8/12 = ₹16,000. The remaining ₹8,000 is unearned revenue (a liability). ₹14,000 comes from counting 7 months; ₹24,000 is the trap of treating all the cash as revenue.

facc-w3-q5.question: A company forgot to record March's ₹12,000 electricity bill (to be paid in April). What is the effect on the 31 March statements?
options: Profit is overstated by ₹12,000 and liabilities understated by ₹12,000
Profit is understated by ₹12,000 and liabilities overstated by ₹12,000
Profit is correct, only cash is wrong
Profit is overstated by ₹12,000 and assets overstated by ₹12,000
facc-w3-q5.explanation: The missing entry is an expense of ₹12,000 and an outstanding liability of ₹12,000. Without the expense, profit (and equity) is ₹12,000 too high and liabilities ₹12,000 too low. Cash is unaffected because payment is in April — the 'only cash is wrong' option gets this backwards.

facc-w3-q6.question: During the year a firm collected ₹5,00,000 in cash from customers, of which ₹40,000 related to last year's sales. At year-end ₹60,000 from this year's sales is still receivable. It paid ₹3,20,000 in cash for expenses, of which ₹10,000 is prepaid for next year; and ₹25,000 of expenses are still outstanding. What is this year's profit on the accrual basis?
facc-w3-q6.explanation: Revenue = 5,00,000 − 40,000 (last year's) + 60,000 (receivable) = 5,20,000. Expenses = 3,20,000 − 10,000 (prepaid) + 25,000 (outstanding) = 3,35,000. Profit = ₹1,85,000. ₹1,80,000 is the cash-basis answer; ₹2,25,000 comes from not removing last year's ₹40,000; ₹1,65,000 from adding the prepayment instead of subtracting it.

facc-w4-q1.question: Purchase prices rose steadily all year. Comparing FIFO with weighted average, which statement is correct?
options: Weighted average gives higher closing inventory and higher profit
Both methods always give the same profit
FIFO gives higher closing inventory and higher profit
FIFO gives higher COGS and lower profit
facc-w4-q1.explanation: Under FIFO the older, cheaper units go to COGS first and the newer, dearer units remain in closing inventory. So with rising prices FIFO gives lower COGS and higher profit. The last option would be true if prices were falling.

facc-w4-q2.question: Opening inventory 50 units @ ₹200, purchase 1: 150 units @ ₹220, purchase 2: 100 units @ ₹250. 220 units were sold in the period. What is the cost of goods sold under FIFO?
facc-w4-q2.explanation: FIFO: 50 × 200 = 10,000; 150 × 220 = 33,000; remaining 20 × 250 = 5,000 ⇒ COGS = ₹48,000 (closing = 80 × 250 = 20,000). ₹49,867 is weighted average (68,000 ÷ 300 × 220), ₹51,400 is LIFO (newest units first), which Ind AS does not allow, and ₹44,000 is the trap of costing every unit at ₹200.

facc-w4-q3.question: Opening 40 units @ ₹100 and a purchase of 60 units @ ₹110. 70 units are sold. What is the value of closing inventory under the weighted average (periodic) method?
facc-w4-q3.explanation: Average = (4,000 + 6,600) ÷ 100 = ₹106 per unit. Closing 30 units × 106 = ₹3,180. ₹3,150 comes from a simple average of the prices (105), ignoring the units; ₹3,300 is the FIFO answer and ₹3,000 the LIFO answer.

facc-w4-q4.question: A machine is bought for ₹5,00,000 with a useful life of 5 years and a residual value of ₹50,000. Under the straight line method, what is its carrying amount after 2 years?
facc-w4-q4.explanation: Annual depreciation = (5,00,000 − 50,000) ÷ 5 = 90,000. Two years give 1,80,000 ⇒ carrying amount = ₹3,20,000. ₹3,00,000 comes from ignoring the residual value (1,00,000 per year).

facc-w4-q5.question: A delivery van costing ₹5,00,000 is depreciated at 20% on the written-down value method. What is the depreciation for the third year?
facc-w4-q5.explanation: Year 1: 5,00,000 × 20% = 1,00,000 (leaving 4,00,000). Year 2: 4,00,000 × 20% = 80,000 (leaving 3,20,000). Year 3: 3,20,000 × 20% = ₹64,000. ₹1,00,000 is the trap of applying the rate to cost every year; ₹51,200 is year four.

facc-w4-q6.question: At year-end a company faces three court cases. Case A: ₹4,00,000, lawyers say losing is probable and the amount is reliable. Case B: ₹6,00,000, losing is only possible. Case C: ₹2,00,000, the chance of losing is remote. Under Ind AS 37, how much is recognised as a provision and how much is disclosed as a contingent liability?
facc-w4-q6.explanation: A is probable and measurable ⇒ a ₹4,00,000 provision (expense + liability). B is possible ⇒ ₹6,00,000 appears only in the notes as a contingent liability. C is remote ⇒ not even disclosed. Disclosing ₹8,00,000 is the trap of including the remote case; a ₹10,00,000 provision comes from treating possible as probable.

facc-w5-q1.question: A company's profit before tax is ₹12,00,000 and the tax rate is 25%. What is the profit after tax?
facc-w5-q1.explanation: Tax = 12,00,000 × 25% = 3,00,000; PAT = 12,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹9,00,000. ₹3,00,000 is just the tax, and ₹15,00,000 is the trap of adding the tax instead of subtracting it.

facc-w5-q2.question: Which statement about a dividend paid to equity shareholders is correct?
options: It is an expense in the P&L and reduces PAT
It becomes a liability at the start of the year
It is a distribution of profit that reduces retained earnings
facc-w5-q2.explanation: A dividend is not a cost of earning profit; it shares out profit already earned among the owners. So it is deducted from retained earnings after PAT. The first option is the most common trap — a dividend does not change PAT.

facc-w5-q3.question: A company's opening retained earnings are ₹5,00,000. This year's PAT is ₹3,00,000 and a dividend of ₹1.5 per share was paid on 80,000 equity shares. What are closing retained earnings?
facc-w5-q3.explanation: Dividend = 80,000 × 1.5 = 1,20,000. Closing = 5,00,000 + 3,00,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹6,80,000. ₹8,00,000 comes from forgetting the dividend, ₹1,80,000 from forgetting the opening balance, and ₹9,20,000 from adding the dividend.

facc-w5-q4.question: Which of these transactions does NOT change the business's **total assets**?
options: Took a new loan from the bank
facc-w5-q4.explanation: Machinery for cash: one asset (machinery) rises and another (cash) falls by the same amount — the total is unchanged. A loan and new capital raise assets; paying a creditor reduces both cash and liabilities, so total assets fall.

facc-w5-q5.question: A company's PBT is ₹10,00,000, the tax rate is 25%, and it paid a dividend of ₹3,00,000 during the year. What is the dividend payout ratio?
facc-w5-q5.explanation: PAT = 10,00,000 × 75% = 7,50,000. Payout = 3,00,000 ÷ 7,50,000 = 40%. 30% comes from dividing by PBT; 60% is the retention ratio, not the payout.

facc-w5-q6.question: A business has Assets ₹6,00,000 = Liabilities ₹2,00,000 + Equity ₹4,00,000. Then: (a) it buys inventory of ₹50,000 on credit, (b) pays a supplier ₹20,000 in cash, (c) sells inventory costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 cash. What are total assets now?
facc-w5-q6.explanation: (a) inventory +50,000, payables +50,000. (b) cash −20,000, payables −20,000. (c) cash +45,000, inventory −30,000, equity +15,000. Assets = 6,00,000 + 50,000 − 20,000 + 45,000 − 30,000 = ₹6,45,000 = liabilities 2,30,000 + equity 4,15,000. ₹6,75,000 comes from forgetting to remove the inventory sold; ₹6,65,000 from forgetting the cash paid to the supplier.

facc-w6-q1.question: In a manufacturing company's balance sheet, which of these items is a **current asset**?
options: A long-term investment in another company's shares
facc-w6-q1.explanation: Inventory is sold and turned into cash within the normal operating cycle, so it is a current asset. Land and goodwill last for years, and a long-term investment is held for the long run too — all three are non-current.

facc-w6-q2.question: A company's items: inventories ₹3,00,000; trade receivables ₹2,50,000; cash ₹1,00,000; prepaid expenses ₹20,000; trade payables ₹2,80,000; short-term borrowings ₹1,20,000; long-term borrowings ₹5,00,000; PPE ₹9,00,000. What is the working capital?
facc-w6-q2.explanation: Current assets = 3,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,00,000 + 20,000 = 6,70,000. Current liabilities = 2,80,000 + 1,20,000 = 4,00,000. WC = ₹2,70,000. −₹2,30,000 comes from treating long-term borrowings as current too; ₹2,50,000 from leaving out prepaid expenses; ₹3,90,000 from leaving out short-term borrowings.

facc-w6-q3.question: A company issued 50,000 equity shares (face value ₹10) at ₹60 per share and received the full amount. How much goes to securities premium?
options: ₹0 — the premium becomes income in the P&L
facc-w6-q3.explanation: Premium per share = 60 − 10 = ₹50; total = 50,000 × 50 = ₹25,00,000 (other equity). Share capital = 50,000 × 10 = 5,00,000, and total cash is 30,00,000. The premium is shareholders' capital, not income — so the last option is wrong.

facc-w6-q4.question: What does the 'consolidated balance sheet' in an annual report show?
options: Only the parent company's own assets and liabilities
The total of the last five years' balance sheets
The parent and its subsidiaries combined as one group
Only the subsidiaries' figures, without the parent
facc-w6-q4.explanation: Consolidated statements combine the parent and its subsidiaries as one economic entity (removing transactions between them). The parent's own figures are in the standalone statements — the first option describes standalone.

facc-w6-q5.question: On 31 March a company has a ₹10,00,000 term loan repayable in annual instalments of ₹2,00,000; the first instalment is due within the next 12 months. How is it shown in the balance sheet?
facc-w6-q5.explanation: The part due within the next 12 months (₹2,00,000) is a current maturity — it goes in current liabilities. The remaining ₹8,00,000 is non-current borrowings. Showing the whole loan as non-current is the most common mistake, and it makes working capital look bigger.

facc-w6-q6.question: A company has total assets of ₹50,00,000, non-current liabilities of ₹15,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹9,00,000. It has 1,50,000 equity shares (face value ₹10). What is the book value per share?
facc-w6-q6.explanation: Total equity = 50,00,000 − 15,00,000 − 9,00,000 = 26,00,000 (share capital 15,00,000 + other equity 11,00,000). Book value = 26,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = ₹17.33. ₹33.33 is the trap of dividing total assets by shares (liabilities do not belong to owners); ₹10 is the face value; ₹7.33 is only other equity per share.

facc-w7-q1.question: A company's revenue is ₹8,00,000 and cost of goods sold is ₹4,80,000. What is the gross profit margin?
facc-w7-q1.explanation: GP = 8,00,000 − 4,80,000 = 3,20,000. Margin = 3,20,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 40%. 66.7% comes from dividing GP by COGS (that is the markup, not the margin); 60% is COGS as a share of revenue.

facc-w7-q2.question: What must be subtracted to go from EBITDA to EBIT?
facc-w7-q2.explanation: EBIT = EBITDA − D&A; the 'DA' drops out of the name itself. Finance costs are subtracted after EBIT (on the way to PBT), and tax after PBT — both are lower steps of the ladder.

facc-w7-q3.question: A company's PAT is ₹6,00,000, tax expense ₹2,00,000, finance costs ₹1,50,000 and depreciation ₹2,50,000. There is no other income or exceptional item. What is EBITDA?
facc-w7-q3.explanation: Add back from the bottom: PAT 6,00,000 + tax 2,00,000 = PBT 8,00,000; + finance 1,50,000 = EBIT 9,50,000; + depreciation 2,50,000 = EBITDA ₹12,00,000. ₹9,50,000 is EBIT (depreciation not added back) and ₹8,00,000 is only PBT.

facc-w7-q4.question: A company: revenue from operations ₹60,00,000; other income (FD interest) ₹4,00,000; total expenses ₹50,00,000, including depreciation of ₹3,00,000 and finance costs of ₹2,00,000. If EBITDA excludes other income, what is EBITDA?
facc-w7-q4.explanation: Operating expenses (without D&A and finance costs) = 50,00,000 − 3,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 45,00,000. EBITDA = 60,00,000 − 45,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. ₹19,00,000 comes from adding other income (not this question's convention), and ₹14,00,000 is PBT (64,00,000 − 50,00,000).

facc-w7-q5.question: A trading company: revenue ₹10,00,000; purchases of stock-in-trade ₹7,00,000; opening inventory ₹1,50,000; closing inventory ₹2,00,000. What is the gross profit?
facc-w7-q5.explanation: COGS = 1,50,000 + 7,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 6,50,000 (change in inventories = opening − closing = −50,000). GP = 10,00,000 − 6,50,000 = ₹3,50,000. ₹3,00,000 comes from ignoring the inventory change, and ₹2,50,000 from using the wrong sign (+50,000) for the change.

facc-w7-q6.question: A company's PAT is ₹45,00,000 and its preference dividend is ₹5,00,000. It had 8,00,000 equity shares on 1 April and issued 4,00,000 new shares on 1 October (financial year 1 April – 31 March). What is basic EPS?
facc-w7-q6.explanation: The new shares were outstanding for 6 months: weighted shares = 8,00,000 + 4,00,000 × 6/12 = 10,00,000. Profit for equity = 45,00,000 − 5,00,000 = 40,00,000. EPS = ₹4.00. ₹3.33 comes from using the 12,00,000 year-end shares, ₹4.50 from not deducting the preference dividend, ₹5.00 from using only the opening shares.

facc-w8-q1.question: The business paid staff a salary of ₹15,000 in cash. What is the correct journal entry?
facc-w8-q1.explanation: Salary expense rises ⇒ debit; cash (an asset) falls ⇒ credit. The first option is reversed. Capital would be debited if the owner took money for himself (drawings) — staff salary is a business expense.

facc-w8-q2.question: Which of these accounts normally has a **debit** balance?
facc-w8-q2.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's equity, so an increase in drawings is a debit and the normal balance is debit. Trade payables (liability), share capital (equity) and revenue all increase with a credit. Treating drawings as a credit like equity is the common trap.

facc-w8-q3.question: Goods were sold to Ramesh on credit last month. Today Ramesh paid ₹20,000 in cash. What is the correct entry?
facc-w8-q3.explanation: Cash (an asset) rises ⇒ debit; the receivable from Ramesh (an asset) falls ⇒ credit. Crediting Sales is the big trap — the sale was already recorded last month, and recording it again would double the revenue.

facc-w8-q4.question: The cash account has an opening balance of ₹12,000 debit. During the month receipts are ₹45,000 and ₹8,000; payments are ₹20,000, ₹30,000 and ₹4,500. What is the cash account balance at month-end?
facc-w8-q4.explanation: Debit side = 12,000 + 45,000 + 8,000 = 65,000; credit side = 20,000 + 30,000 + 4,500 = 54,500. Balance = ₹10,500 debit (the debit side is bigger). ₹1,500 credit comes from forgetting the opening balance, and ₹15,000 from leaving out one payment (4,500).

facc-w8-q5.question: Which of these errors does **not** cause a difference in the trial balance totals?
options: Only the debit side of an entry was posted
A ledger account was totalled wrongly
₹500 was posted as the debit and ₹5,000 as the credit
The purchase of new machinery was debited to the Repairs account
facc-w8-q5.explanation: Debiting machinery to Repairs is an error of principle: debit and credit are still equal, just in the wrong type of account — the TB agrees, but profit and assets are understated. The other three errors make one side differ from the other, so the TB shows a difference.

facc-w8-q6.question: A trial balance has a debit total of ₹2,45,000 and a credit total of ₹2,52,000. Two errors are found: (a) rent of ₹3,500 was correctly credited to the cash account but never posted to the Rent account; (b) a sales return of ₹1,750 was posted to the credit side of the Sales Returns account instead of the debit side. After correcting both, what is the trial balance total?
facc-w8-q6.explanation: (a) Add the rent debit: debit 2,45,000 + 3,500 = 2,48,500. (b) Remove the sales return from the credit side and put it on the debit side: debit 2,48,500 + 1,750 = 2,50,250; credit 2,52,000 − 1,750 = 2,50,250. Both agree. ₹2,48,500 comes from fixing only the first error; ₹2,53,750 from adding the return to the credit side instead of removing it.

facc-w9-q1.question: In the indirect method, why is depreciation added back to profit?
options: It is a non-cash expense — it reduced profit but no cash left the business this year
Depreciation brings cash into the company
To make the tax expense look smaller
facc-w9-q1.explanation: The cash for the machine left when it was bought (under investing); depreciation only spreads that cost over the years. It reduced profit without moving cash, so it is added back. It is not a source of cash — that is the most common misunderstanding.

facc-w9-q2.question: During the year trade receivables rose from ₹2,00,000 to ₹2,80,000. When computing CFO by the indirect method, what do you do with this?
options: Ignore it, it is a balance sheet item
facc-w9-q2.explanation: Higher receivables mean some sales are in profit but their cash has not arrived. So subtract the ₹80,000 increase. You would add it if receivables fell (old dues being collected).

facc-w9-q3.question: A proprietorship (ignore tax) has net profit of ₹2,00,000. Depreciation ₹40,000; inventory rose by ₹30,000; trade payables rose by ₹20,000; trade receivables rose by ₹25,000. What is cash from operating activities?
facc-w9-q3.explanation: 2,00,000 + 40,000 − 30,000 (inventory ↑) + 20,000 (payables ↑) − 25,000 (receivables ↑) = ₹2,05,000. ₹2,75,000 comes from reversing the working capital signs, ₹1,25,000 from subtracting depreciation, and ₹2,40,000 from ignoring working capital.

facc-w9-q4.question: A company sold old equipment for ₹65,000; its carrying amount was ₹50,000, so a ₹15,000 gain appeared in the P&L. What is the correct treatment in the cash flow statement?
options: Add ₹15,000 in CFO, because cash came in
Subtract ₹15,000 in CFO; show the full ₹65,000 as an inflow under investing activities
facc-w9-q4.explanation: Selling equipment is an investing activity, so the full ₹65,000 of cash goes under investing. The ₹15,000 gain is already in profit — subtract it in CFO, or it gets counted twice. Ignoring the gain is exactly that double-counting trap.

facc-w9-q5.question: A company's tax expense for the year is ₹1,50,000. Its tax payable had an opening balance of ₹40,000 and a closing balance of ₹55,000. How much income tax was paid in cash during the year?
facc-w9-q5.explanation: Tax paid = opening 40,000 + expense 1,50,000 − closing 55,000 = ₹1,35,000. The payable rose, meaning not all of the expense has been paid yet. ₹1,65,000 comes from swapping opening and closing; ₹1,50,000 from assuming the expense was all paid.

facc-w9-q6.question: A company: PBT ₹8,00,000; depreciation ₹1,20,000; finance costs ₹50,000; interest income ₹20,000; trade receivables rose by ₹70,000; inventory fell by ₹30,000; trade payables fell by ₹40,000; income tax paid ₹1,80,000. Using the course convention (interest paid in financing, interest received in investing), what is CFO?
facc-w9-q6.explanation: 8,00,000 + 1,20,000 + 50,000 − 20,000 = 9,50,000. WC: −70,000 + 30,000 − 40,000 = −80,000 ⇒ 8,70,000. Tax: − 1,80,000 ⇒ ₹6,90,000. ₹8,70,000 comes from forgetting tax, ₹7,70,000 from adding the fall in payables (it should be subtracted), and ₹6,60,000 from not adjusting finance costs and interest income.

facc-w10-q1.question: A manufacturing company paid a dividend of ₹5,00,000 in cash to its shareholders. Where does this appear in the cash flow statement?
options: Nowhere, because it is not a P&L item
facc-w10-q1.explanation: A dividend is a return to owners, so it is a financing outflow. It is not in the P&L, but cash did leave — so it must appear in the cash flow statement. The operating trap comes from linking dividends with profit.

facc-w10-q2.question: A company bought shares of another company for ₹8,00,000 as a long-term investment. Which activity does this cash flow belong to?
options: It does not appear in the cash flow statement
facc-w10-q2.explanation: Buying another company's shares is an investment ⇒ an investing outflow. It would be financing if the company issued or bought back its **own** shares — that is the most common confusion.

facc-w10-q3.question: During the year a company: received ₹5,00,000 from issuing new shares; took a new loan of ₹2,00,000; repaid an old loan of ₹3,00,000; paid dividends of ₹1,20,000; paid interest of ₹60,000. Keeping interest paid in financing, what is net cash from financing activities?
facc-w10-q3.explanation: 5,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 3,00,000 − 1,20,000 − 60,000 = ₹2,20,000. ₹2,80,000 comes from putting interest in operating, ₹3,40,000 from leaving out the dividend, and ₹11,80,000 from adding every amount (treating outflows as plus).

facc-w10-q4.question: A company's CFO is ₹4,20,000, CFI is −₹6,50,000 and CFF is ₹1,80,000. Opening cash and cash equivalents were ₹1,10,000. What are closing cash and cash equivalents?
facc-w10-q4.explanation: Net change = 4,20,000 − 6,50,000 + 1,80,000 = −50,000. Closing = 1,10,000 − 50,000 = ₹60,000. −₹50,000 is only the net change (opening balance forgotten), ₹1,60,000 comes from reversing the sign of the net change, and ₹13,60,000 from treating CFI as positive.

facc-w10-q5.question: A company's CFO is ₹9,00,000. During the year it spent ₹5,50,000 on PPE, received ₹50,000 from selling old assets, and paid a dividend of ₹1,00,000. Using the definition FCF = CFO − capital expenditure, what is free cash flow?
facc-w10-q5.explanation: By the definition, subtract only capex: 9,00,000 − 5,50,000 = ₹3,50,000. ₹4,00,000 comes from netting asset sale proceeds against capex (a different definition), and ₹2,50,000 from also subtracting the dividend — a dividend is a use of FCF, it does not reduce FCF.

facc-w10-q6.question: A company's opening net PPE is ₹20,00,000 and closing net PPE is ₹23,00,000. Depreciation for the year was ₹2,50,000. An asset with a carrying amount of ₹1,00,000 was sold for ₹70,000 cash. If there are no other investing items, what is net cash from investing activities?
facc-w10-q6.explanation: Purchases = 23,00,000 − 20,00,000 + 2,50,000 + 1,00,000 = 6,50,000. CFI = −6,50,000 + 70,000 = −₹5,80,000. −₹6,50,000 comes from forgetting the sale proceeds, −₹3,00,000 from using only the net change in PPE, and −₹5,50,000 from treating the carrying amount (1,00,000) as the cash inflow.

facc-w11-q1.question: A company has current assets of ₹6,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹4,00,000. What is the current ratio?
facc-w11-q1.explanation: Current ratio = 6,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 1.50. 0.67 comes from inverting the ratio (CL ÷ CA), and 0.50 from dividing working capital (2,00,000) by CL.

facc-w11-q2.question: A company has current assets of ₹6,00,000, including inventories of ₹2,00,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹20,000. Current liabilities are ₹4,00,000. What is the quick ratio?
facc-w11-q2.explanation: Quick assets = 6,00,000 − 2,00,000 − 20,000 = 3,80,000. Quick ratio = 3,80,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = 0.95. 1.00 comes from removing only inventory and forgetting prepaid expenses; 1.50 is the current ratio.

facc-w11-q3.question: A company: long-term borrowings ₹12,00,000; short-term borrowings ₹3,00,000; equity share capital ₹10,00,000; other equity ₹15,00,000. Taking debt as all borrowings, what is the debt-equity ratio?
facc-w11-q3.explanation: Debt = 12,00,000 + 3,00,000 = 15,00,000; equity = 10,00,000 + 15,00,000 = 25,00,000. D/E = 0.60. 0.48 comes from leaving out short-term borrowings, and 1.50 from using only share capital as equity.

facc-w11-q4.question: A company's EBIT is ₹9,00,000 and its finance costs are ₹1,50,000. What is the interest coverage ratio?
facc-w11-q4.explanation: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = 9,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 6 times. 5 times comes from using PBT (7,50,000) — interest has already been deducted in PBT. 0.17 comes from inverting the ratio.

facc-w11-q5.question: A company has current assets of ₹4,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹2,00,000 (current ratio 2.00). It pays ₹50,000 of trade payables in cash. What happens to the current ratio?
facc-w11-q5.explanation: Both sides fall by 50,000: 3,50,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 2.33. When a ratio is above 1, taking the same amount off the numerator and denominator raises it. 1.75 comes from reducing only cash, and 2.67 from reducing only payables — changing just one side is wrong.

facc-w11-q6.question: A company's current ratio is 2.5 and its working capital is ₹6,00,000. Inventories are ₹3,00,000 and there are no prepaid expenses. What is the quick ratio?
facc-w11-q6.explanation: CA = 2.5 × CL and CA − CL = 6,00,000 ⇒ 1.5 × CL = 6,00,000 ⇒ CL = 4,00,000, CA = 10,00,000. Quick = (10,00,000 − 3,00,000) ÷ 4,00,000 = 1.75. 2.50 is just the current ratio, 0.75 is inventory ÷ CL, and 1.17 is the trap of dividing quick assets by working capital.

facc-w12-q1.question: A company's revenue is ₹30,00,000 and PAT is ₹4,50,000. What is the net profit margin?
facc-w12-q1.explanation: NPM = 4,50,000 ÷ 30,00,000 = 15%. 6.67 comes from inverting the ratio (revenue ÷ PAT), and 85% is the part that did not become profit.

facc-w12-q2.question: A company's COGS is ₹36,00,000. Opening inventory is ₹5,00,000 and closing inventory ₹7,00,000. A year = 365 days. Roughly how many days inventory outstanding (DIO) is that?
facc-w12-q2.explanation: Average inventory = (5,00,000 + 7,00,000) ÷ 2 = 6,00,000. Turnover = 36,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 6 times. DIO = 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 60.8 ≈ 61 days. 6 is the turnover, not days; 71 days comes from using only closing inventory and 51 days from using only opening inventory.

facc-w12-q3.question: A company's PAT is ₹5,00,000. Equity was ₹18,00,000 at the start of the year and ₹22,00,000 at the end. What is ROE on average equity?
facc-w12-q3.explanation: Average equity = (18,00,000 + 22,00,000) ÷ 2 = 20,00,000. ROE = 5,00,000 ÷ 20,00,000 = 25%. 22.7% comes from using only closing equity, 27.8% from only opening equity, and 12.5% from adding the two without dividing by 2.

facc-w12-q4.question: All of a company's sales are on credit: revenue ₹73,00,000. Trade receivables were ₹10,00,000 at the start of the year and ₹14,00,000 at the end. A year = 365 days. What is DSO on average receivables?
facc-w12-q4.explanation: Average receivables = (10,00,000 + 14,00,000) ÷ 2 = 12,00,000. DSO = 12,00,000 ÷ 73,00,000 × 365 = 60 days. 70 days comes from closing and 50 days from opening receivables; 6.08 is the receivables turnover (how many times), not days.

facc-w12-q5.question: A retailer has DIO of 45 days, DSO of 30 days and DPO of 40 days. How many days is the cash conversion cycle?
facc-w12-q5.explanation: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO = 45 + 30 − 40 = 35 days. 115 days comes from adding all three — supplier credit (DPO) delays the cash outflow, so it is subtracted. 55 and 25 come from subtracting the wrong term.

facc-w12-q6.question: A company has a net profit margin of 8%, asset turnover of 2 and an equity multiplier of 1.5. It takes on more debt: the equity multiplier becomes 2.5, extra interest cuts the net profit margin to 6%, and asset turnover stays at 2. What is the new ROE?
facc-w12-q6.explanation: DuPont: new ROE = 6% × 2 × 2.5 = 30% (before it was 8% × 2 × 1.5 = 24%). 40% comes from forgetting the fall in margin (8% → 6%); 12% is only ROA (NPM × asset turnover). Note: ROE rose, but only through leverage — risk rose too.
